alt: Three kinds of precedent. Binding precedent must be followed when it comes from a court above (or sometimes the same court) and the material facts are sufficiently similar. Persuasive precedent, from lower courts, obiter dicta, dissents, the Privy Council or other common law countries, may be followed. Original precedent is made where no earlier decision exists.
caption: Binding must be followed, persuasive may be, and original precedent fills a gap.

alt: The ratio decidendi is the binding legal principle; obiter dicta are other remarks and only persuasive. In R v Howe (1987) the ratio was that duress is no defence to murder, with an obiter remark that it should not cover attempted murder either; in R v Gotts (1992) the House of Lords followed that obiter remark.
caption: An obiter remark in Howe became the rule in Gotts.

alt: The courts from top to bottom: the Supreme Court binds all below and may depart from its own decisions; the Court of Appeal Civil Division is bound by itself subject to Young v Bristol Aeroplane, the Criminal Division generally so; the Divisional Courts; the High Court, which binds lower courts but not other High Court judges; and the Crown Court, County Court and magistrates’ courts, which create no binding precedent.
caption: Each court binds those below it; only the Supreme Court may freely depart from its own decisions.

alt: A timeline of Practice Statement cases: Conway v Rimmer (1968); Herrington (1972) overruling Addie v Dumbreck; Knuller v DPP (1972) refusing to overrule Shaw v DPP; R v Shivpuri (1986) overruling Anderton v Ryan; R v G (2003) overruling R v Caldwell; and Austin v Southwark (2010) confirming the Statement applies to the Supreme Court.
caption: The power is real but used sparingly, as Knuller shows.

alt: The Court of Appeal Civil Division follows its own decisions except, under Young v Bristol Aeroplane, where its own decisions conflict, where a later House of Lords or Supreme Court decision conflicts, or where the earlier decision was per incuriam. Lord Denning’s call for freedom in Davis v Johnson was rejected; the Criminal Division may depart where liberty is at stake (Taylor; Gould).
caption: Three Young exceptions for the Civil Division; extra flexibility for the Criminal Division.

alt: Four stages of law reporting: Year Books from the late thirteenth century, private reports, The Law Reports of the Incorporated Council of Law Reporting from 1865, and neutral citations since 2001. Five reasons for reporting: an accurate record, advice to clients, identifying binding authority, consistency and certainty, and accessibility supporting the rule of law.
caption: Reliable reports are what make a system of binding precedent workable.

alt: The High Court judge is bound by the Court of Appeal if the material facts are sufficiently similar. She may distinguish on the material facts, or follow while criticising the decision to invite an appeal; she cannot overrule it. In the long term the Court of Appeal or the Supreme Court can change the rule.
caption: Distinguish or follow and criticise; only a higher court can overrule.
